These findings support a branch-aware audit and a scoped negative result, not demonstrated routing superiority. Independent budgets, selected-support validation and net utility under a satisfied SLA remain open.
item.dc:creator: Juan S. Santillana

item.title: Turbo-GMM: FlashAttention-Inspired GPU-Accelerated Gaussian Mixture Model
item.description: arXiv:2611.02449v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Expectation-maximization (EM) for Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) requires scoring $N$ data points against $K$ mixture components. Prior fused GPU implementations, notably Flash-GMM, eliminate materialization of the $N \times K$ responsibility matrix but traverse the component dimension twice to compute normalization terms and accumulate sufficient statistics. We introduce Turbo-GMM, a single-sweep fused EM kernel that completes responsibility normalization and sufficient-statistic accumulation within one traversal of the component dimension. By retaining the complete component axis on chip, Turbo-GMM avoids the second score computation required by the released two-sweep Flash-GMM implementation. Its applicability is limited by register pressure, occupancy, and the component and feature dimensions, making it particularly suitable for large datasets with relatively small numbers of components. For larger configurations, Turbo-GMM employs a two-pass fallback following the established fused design. We establish algebraic equivalence to standard EM in real arithmetic and evaluate sixteen configurations on an NVIDIA A100. Under the reported benchmarking protocol, Turbo-GMM achieves a median $2.15\times$ speedup over the evaluated Flash-GMM implementation and up to $5.3\times$ and $9.9\times$ over PyTorch and \texttt{scikit-learn}, respectively. The results demonstrate the potential of single-sweep component traversal while identifying on-chip resource constraints as the principal limitation of this approach.
item.dc:creator: Momin Abbas, Sadia Asif, Asad Ul Haq, Kaoutar El Maghraoui

item.title: TLAPS-Bench: Formally Proving Correctness of Real-World System Specifications with TLA+ Proof System
item.description: arXiv:2611.02849v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: TLAPS-Bench is a benchmark and execution harness for constructing machine-checked proofs for real-world system specifications in TLA+ with agentic AI. Proving correctness of complex system specifications requires discovering inductive invariants, reasoning about intricate state transitions, and decomposing proofs into tractable obligations. TLAPS-Bench provides a proof harness that supports iterative proof development atop the TLA+ Proof System (TLAPS), where agents are equipped with proof tools and libraries, with safeguards against reward hacking. Using the harness, we have employed AI agents to prove desired properties for important system specifications that were not proved before, spanning cache coherence, Byzantine consensus, and write-ahead logs. TLAPS-Bench contains 265 proof targets (each encodes a property to prove) from 95 TLA+ specifications of real-world systems. We evaluated frontier AI agents, represented by Codex with GPT models, on a subset of 70 proof targets across 12 specifications. The highest-scoring model, GPT-6.1 Sol (max), proved 31 (44.3%) proof targets. The results show challenges and opportunities in end-to-end proof development.
item.dc:creator: Qian Cheng, Ruize Tang, Saad Mohammad Rafid Pial, Zhizhen Cathy Cai, Yiming Su, Jackson Clark, Munim Thahmid, Mahdiya Rahman Sukanya, Chris Newcombe, Igor Konnov, Stephan Merz, Xudong Sun, Murat Demirbas, Yu Huang, Markus Alexander Kuppe, Tianyin Xu

item.title: Low-rank corrections to a shared reference Jacobian for GPU-parallel AC $N\!-\!1$ contingency analysis
item.description: arXiv:2611.03012v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Contingency analysis repeatedly solves the power-flow equations under many single-element outages, an increasingly demanding workload as operating margins tighten and renewable variability grows. Graphics processing units (GPUs) are attractive for this task, but a change in topology alters the sparsity pattern of the Jacobian, preventing the uniform batched factorization on which efficient GPU solvers rely. This paper presents a GPU-parallel Newton--Raphson solver for $N\!-\!1$ contingency analysis that separates the change in operating state from the change in topology. A single reference Jacobian is inverted once and reused across all contingencies. Each topology change is expressed as a low-rank Woodbury correction, while the residual state-dependent perturbation is handled by an inner iterative solve, a truncated Neumann series or the biconjugate gradient stabilized method. We analyze the spectral radius and condition number of the resulting iteration matrices and show that the reference Jacobian is an effective preconditioner. On transmission-scale benchmarks, the method attains per-topology solve times competitive with an optimized 80-core central processing unit baseline, with the low-rank correction accounting for approximately 1--2\% of the workload. This makes GPU-parallel $N\!-\!1$ contingency analysis feasible at transmission scale without per-topology refactorization.
item.dc:creator: Marc Hunkem\"oller, Nico Westerbeck, Joost van Dijk, Lars Schewe, Dirk Witthaut

item.title: Towards a Trustworthy and Governable Internet of Agentics: An Architectural Perspective on Protocols, Systems, and Services
item.description: arXiv:2611.03066v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language model applications are increasingly being organized as tool-using and multi-agent workflows rather than as isolated chat interfaces. This perspective paper examines the architectural problem that follows from that shift: agents may reason, invoke tools, and delegate work, but dependable deployment still requires interoperability across frameworks, runtimes, data boundaries, and organizational control domains. We study this problem through the lens of the \emph{Internet of Agentics} (IoA), an emerging service-computing view in which heterogeneous agents are treated as governable service participants rather than only as stand-alone model endpoints. The paper organizes the landscape as a three-layer progression: from today's fragmented agent ecosystem, to interoperable agents, and ultimately to trustworthy and governable autonomy. First, it examines the protocol stack centered on the Agentic AI Foundation, including MCP for agent--tool interaction; A2A for agent--agent coordination; AGENTS.md and Skills-style procedural manifests; and discovery, transport, and trust mechanisms such as AGNTCY and SLIM. Second, it reviews the systems abstractions that make agents deployable as service components, including logical agent architectures, orchestration patterns, gateways, registries, runtime control loops, and hardware-aware inference infrastructure. Third, it situates these developments within services computing, arguing that agentic systems reinterpret classical concerns from SOA and microservices---discovery, composition, governance, pricing, and trust---at the level of cognitive capabilities rather than deterministic functions.
item.dc:creator: Haoyi Xiong, Yi Liu, Jiang Bian, Peng Diao, Bin Zhu, Tingting Hu, Yi Wang, Sumi Helal

item.title: Dynamic Coalition Formation Under Capacity Constraints: A Regime-Switching Value-Investing Game
item.description: arXiv:2611.03137v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Edge computing service deployment requires the Network Operator (NO) and Service Providers (SPs) to coordinate investment and resource allocation under uncertain demand. This paper develops an audit-based service management framework for daily coalition formation with fixed capacity and service-level agreement (SLA) reservations. A two-stage coalitional game separates infrastructure investment from operational participation. Demand follows a Geometric Random Walk (GRW), and SPs apply an ordered admission and suspension rule using reported marginal contributions. With the NO held fixed, the operational coalition value is submodular; mandatory reservations can produce negative Shapley payoffs. We derive a separable benchmark, compute operational Shapley allocations, and give a sufficient condition for convergence to an individual equilibrium. A probabilistic audit mechanism provides a conditional daily truthfulness guarantee under verified settlement and enforceable penalties. For five service classes over three years, the reference run gains 12.4% over static grand-coalition membership and recovers 94.6% of the full-information optimum. Across 30 runs, the median gain is 13.3%. Sensitivity tests examine policy parameters, capacity and alternative demand models. The gain depends on capacity and update order; abundant capacity can make the admission rule underperform static membership.
item.dc:creator: Rosario Patan\`e

item.title: Searching the Plane in the Segment Visibility Model
item.description: arXiv:2611.03161v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study deterministic search by $n \geq 2$ unit-speed robots starting at the origin of the Euclidean plane. We introduce the concept of \emph{segment visibility} whereby a stationary target $x$ at distance $d=\|x\|>0$ is discovered at the first instant $t$ when $x$ belongs to the segment joining a pair of robots at time $t$. Discovery time is compared with the omniscient optimum $d$. We distinguish two knowledge models according to whether the robots know $d$ in advance. For $n=2$ robots, in the \emph{known-$d$} model, we give a symmetric four-phase algorithm and prove that its competitive ratio is optimal: $1+\sqrt3+\pi/6$; the matching lower bound follows from the known-distance two-robot shoreline-search theorem through an explicit reduction to segment detection. For $n=2$ robots, in the \emph{unknown-$d$} model, a three-circle construction and a quantitative initial-path estimate yield the stronger lower bound $\sqrt3+\pi/6+\sqrt{17}/4 \approx3.286425990$, giving an explicit positive cost for not knowing the radius; we also analyze a feasible antipodal-diameter logarithmic-spiral algorithm with optimized ratio $8.928516954\ldots$, thus proving that the competitive ratio when $d$ is unknown is at least $ \sqrt3+\pi/6+\sqrt{17}/4 $ and at most $8.928516954\ldots.$ For $n \geq 3$ robots, the competitive ratio of finding the target is exactly $\sec (\pi/n)$ regardless of whether or not $d$ is known to the robots.
item.dc:creator: Evangelos Kranakis

item.title: Multi-GPU Acceleration of Interface Problems in FEniCS, with Application to Cardiac Modeling
item.description: arXiv:2611.03181v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: GPU acceleration of finite element assembly is well established for standard formulations, but mixed-dimensional problems, in which volumetric subdomains are coupled via lower-dimensional interfaces, remain unsupported in automated frameworks such as FEniCS. We extend cuDOLFINx, a GPU-enabled extension of the DOLFINx finite element framework, to assemble such interface problems on GPUs while preserving the high-level FEniCS programming model. Combined with GPU-resident Krylov solvers and algebraic multigrid preconditioning, this enables end-to-end GPU execution of the EMI (Extracellular--Membrane--Intracellular) model, an elliptic interface problem from cardiac modeling in which many intracellular subdomains are coupled through membranes. We compare the GPU implementation against a CPU-based one through strong and weak scaling experiments on regular and realistic 3D cardiac geometries with up to 8000 cells and 22 million degrees of freedom. In terms of assembly, a single GH200 node is roughly equivalent to two 144-core CPU nodes in strong scaling, and to two to three nodes in weak scaling, depending on geometry. For the linear solver, performance depends on geometry, preconditioning, and problem scale. On the regular geometry, GPU advantages emerge mainly at larger problem sizes and node counts. On the realistic geometry, with the same algebraic multigrid preconditioner for both architectures, the GPU is faster at all tested scales. The implementation is available as open-source software and applies to other problems with interface coupling.
item.dc:creator: Edoardo Centofanti, Benjamin Pachev, Joshua Steyer, James D. Trotter, Pietro Benedusi

item.title: uTECH Turbo-MOVES: The Intersection of Software Architectural Innovation and Sustainable Mobility Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2611.03321v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Transportation is a major source of energy consumption, greenhouse gas emissions, and criteria air pollutants, making efficient emissions estimation essential for environmental planning and policy analyses. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's Motor Vehicle Emission Simulator (MOVES) supports detailed emissions modeling, but its computational demands constrain large-scale scenario analyses. This study introduces uTECH Turbo-MOVES, a software architecture that expedites MOVES computation without modifying its Calculator modules or input/output structure. By combining RunSpec partitioning, container isolation, in-memory intermediate storage, and concurrent workload orchestration, it improves execution efficiency. We evaluate six benchmark cases spanning County, Default, and Project scales and both Emission Inventory and Emission Rates modes. Results demonstrate a measured 5.5x and an estimated 15.3x per-run speedup for Default-scale workloads, and an 84.8x campaign speedup for an eight-county Emission Rates analysis. Although gains vary by workload and hardware configuration, uTECH Turbo-MOVES enables more extensive environmental assessments and transportation policy evaluation.
item.dc:creator: Cafer Avc{\i}, Alireza Yazdiani, Roopak Srinivasan, Megh Khaire, Mohammad Tayarani, H. Oliver Gao

item.title: Scaling global tractography with ExaTract: from large cohorts to ultra-high-resolution datasets
item.description: arXiv:2611.03419v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Global tractography offers a theoretical framework for reconstructing white matter connectivity from diffusion MRI by jointly inferring all streamlines and their consistency with the diffusion signal and underlying anatomical priors. However, its sequential nature and log-linear complexity make it computationally prohibitive at the scales demanded by neuroimaging, from large population cohorts such as the Human Connectome Project (HCP) to ex vivo ultra-high-field acquisitions at mesoscopic resolution. In this work, we present ExaTract, a parallelized spin-glass tractography framework designed for high-performance computing (HPC) architectures. Implemented as an open-source MPI+Kokkos application, ExaTract partitions the tractography domain into spatially overlapping regions processed across distributed memory nodes, with regular synchronization of boundary modifications to preserve global convergence guarantees. We validate ExaTract on both in vivo and ex vivo diffusion MRI data: the complete HCP dataset demonstrates population-scale throughput, while the high-resolution Chenonceau dataset provides the first mesoscopic structural connectome derived from global tractography.
item.dc:creator: Simon Legeay, Felix Matuschke, Bastien Herlin, Jan Andr\'e Reuter, Christophe Destrieux, Markus Axer, Ivy Uszynski, Cyril Poupon

item.title: DistDebug-Bench: Can LLM Agents Diagnose Bugs in Distributed Systems?
item.description: arXiv:2611.03523v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLM agents show strong potential in software engineering tasks such as competitive programming and code synthesis. Existing benchmarks, however, largely focus on small-scale settings such as self-contained Python modules, leaving distributed systems, an essential class of production software, under-examined. We introduce DistDebug-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating agents' ability to diagnose complex-system failures at the code level. It curates 120 high-quality real-world bugs from 11 widely used distributed systems, spanning 5 programming languages and 10 failure patterns. Through an extensive evaluation of state-of-the-art LLMs and agents, we identify substantial gaps between current agents and real-world debugging tasks. A recurring gap is tunnel vision due to a lack of explicit reasoning structure and nondeterminism from inconsistent tool-use scope. The benchmark and evaluator are available at https://github.com/OrderLab/distdebug-bench, with agent traces and a leaderboard at https://distdebug.com.
item.dc:creator: Yuxuan Jiang, Chenglin Liu, John Rose, Mason Miller, Ruthesh Thavamani, Juntao Wu, Yinwei Huang, Jiahao Xu, Peng Huang

item.title: A GPU Engine for Sparse Matrix-Vector Products on $k^2$-Tree-Compressed Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2611.03610v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The $k^2$-tree is a compact representation of Boolean matrices: it stores the recursive hierarchy of their non-empty submatrices, with neither values nor coordinates, and serves rows and columns alike. Its traversal, however, locates the children of each node by rank queries, a chain of dependent irregular loads that leaves a GPU waiting on memory. We implement sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV) on $k^2$-trees for the GPU. Since the traversal does not depend on the vector, the positions of the children are static: we descend the tree one level at a time and obtain them from a parallel prefix sum or from a sampled directory of about 0.1 bits per node. Descending in tiles bounds the temporary memory by the depth of the tree, so the device memory of a product is known before it runs. The same traversal computes right and left products, for one vector or a batch, over the plus-times, Boolean and tropical semirings. We evaluate the engine on an NVIDIA GB10 and an H100 with fourteen Wikidata, Software Heritage, web and social graphs of up to 1.2 billion edges, against cuSPARSE, a grammar-compressed GPU engine and a Boolean CSR. Our results show that the tree is 2.3-27x smaller than the CSR of cuSPARSE and that, with its last internal level cached, a product takes 0.7-2.4x the time of cuSPARSE on the right and 0.27-2.6x on the left. On a 1.2-billion-edge graph, a product needs 1.1 GB on the device, 9x less than cuSPARSE. The engine is memory bounded: the $k^2$-tree is the format of choice when device memory, not time, is the constraint.
item.dc:creator: Francesco Tosoni, Gabriele Mencagli

item.title: QScale: Probabilistic Chained Consensus for Moderate-Scale Systems
item.description: arXiv:2510.01536v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Existing distributed ledger protocols either incur a high communication complexity and are thus suited to systems with a small number of processes (e.g., PBFT), or rely on committee-sampling-based approaches that only work for a very large number of processes (e.g., Algorand). Neither of these lines of work is well-suited for moderate-scale distributed ledgers ranging from a few hundred to a thousand processes, which are common in production (e.g, Redbelly, Sui). The goal of this work is to design a distributed ledger with sub-linear communication complexity per process, sub-quadratic total communication complexity, and low latency for finalizing a block into the ledger, such that it can be used for moderate-scale systems. We propose QScale, a protocol in which every process incurs only $\widetilde{O}(\kappa \sqrt{n})$ communication complexity per-block in expectation, $\widetilde{O}(n\kappa)$ total communication complexity per-block in expectation, and a best-case latency of $O(\kappa)$ rounds while ensuring safety and liveness with overwhelming probability, with $\kappa$ being a small security parameter.
item.dc:creator: Hasan Heydari, Alysson Bessani, Kartik Nayak

item.title: Emulating Heterogeneous Client Execution in Federated Learning
item.description: arXiv:2602.06498v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: FL systems are inherently subject to client heterogeneity arising from differences in hardware capabilities. We propose a realistic evaluation framework for hardware-aware federated learning methods based on lightweight emulation of client hardware. Existing evaluation approaches address this either through small-scale real-device deployments or through trace-driven and probabilistic simulations. The former are difficult to scale and reproduce, while the latter suffer from three compounding sources of uncertainty: the choice of distribution family, the choice of execution-time estimates, and the inability to capture workload-dependent behavior. Our framework reproduces heterogeneous client behavior at execution time, capturing compute capacity, memory-constrained feasibility, and their interaction within a single host system. Unlike fixed-trace or throughput-scaling approaches, the proposed method is workload-aware: the same client population can exhibit different runtime and failure behavior depending on the task under study. We evaluate the fidelity of the approach across multiple workloads and show it preserves relative device performance while accurately reflecting hardware-dependent execution constraints. Compared against direct hardware measurements and benchmark references, the emulation accurately reproduces feasibility and training performance, preserving both relative device ordering and absolute compute times. We demonstrate the importance of workload-aware compute times by evaluating different heterogeneity-management methods across multiple workloads. By coupling emulation with real-world-based device sampling, our framework enables realistic, scalable, and reproducible evaluation of federated learning systems under heterogeneous learning conditions, while providing a practical way to generate workload-specific runtime behavior for large and diverse client populations.
item.dc:creator: Arno Geimer, Beltran Fiz, Dimitris Stripelis

item.title: Pacing Branch Parallelism in LLM Serving
item.description: arXiv:2605.06914v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent methods expose intra-request parallelism in LLM outputs, allowing independent branches to decode concurrently. Existing serving systems execute these branches eagerly or under fixed caps. We show that both are brittle: eager admission inflates the shared decode step, degrading co-batched requests in serial stages, while conservative fixed caps forgo the throughput that motivated exposing branches in the first place. We call the excess step latency caused by admitted branches the \emph{branch externality} and show that the safe width depends on batch composition, context lengths, and accumulated slack, all of which change continuously over a workload trace. We introduce PACE, a per-step admission controller that treats extra branches as opportunistic width, admitted only when the predicted branch externality fits within the batch's current slack budget. Per-step regulation is practical because branch-level scheduling decouples compute from memory: branches share the request's prefix KV, so expanding or contracting width requires no memory reclamation. On Qwen3-32B, PACE improves goodput by $1.77\times$ over serving without branch parallelism and by $1.48\times$ over eager admission while maintaining 99\% SLO attainment. Comparable gains ($1.72$--$2.15\times$) hold on five additional dense and mixture-of-experts models with up to 671B parameters. Code is available at https://github.com/Swapnil-Gandhi/PACE
item.dc:creator: Swapnil Gandhi, Siva Kumar Sastry Hari, William J. Dally, Christos Kozyrakis

item.title: GoodServe: Globally-coordinated Routing of Agentic LLM Inferences for High Goodput
item.description: arXiv:2605.16867v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Agentic applications consume LLM inferences as complete outputs: a code patch or database query is useful only after its last token arrives. Their performance is thus measured by end-to-end deadline satisfaction and goodput, the number of inferences completed within their deadlines. In heterogeneous GPU pools, existing greedy routers favor the fastest or least-loaded instance, often wasting powerful GPUs on requests that could meet their deadlines on weaker ones. Maximizing goodput instead requires globally coordinated routing, informed by uncertain output lengths and dynamic instance performance. We present GoodServe, a goodput-oriented routing system that addresses these challenges through a predict-and-rectify design. A task-gated mixture-of-experts predictor estimates request output lengths, while an EMA-smoothed black-box estimator tracks queuing delays and per-token speeds, accounting for prefix-cache reuse. A just-enough policy routes each request to the weakest instance capable of meeting its deadline and rejects requests that cannot finish on time. Periodic risk checks trigger migration of endangered requests using token IDs, at 7-15 times lower cost than KV-cache transfer. On a four-GPU heterogeneous testbed with three agentic benchmarks, GoodServe achieves the highest goodput across all evaluated SLO levels, improving over the best existing router by up to 31.0%. Its routing overhead remains 5 ms per request at 10,000 requests per second across 512 simulated instances.
item.dc:creator: Boxiao Du, Boning Huangfu, Yizhou Luo, Chen Chen, Zijun Li, Minchen Yu, Xiaoyi Fan, Minyi Guo

item.title: Conflict-Freedom as a Progress Condition
item.description: arXiv:2605.19531v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: An obstruction-free implementation guarantees progress to every operation that is given enough time to take steps in isolation. But, as we show in this paper, the mere presence of concurrent operations alone does not have to prevent progress; only incomplete conflicting (non-commuting) operations may do so. This progress condition, that we call conflict-freedom, is a natural generalization of obstruction-freedom that promises efficient implementations for objects exhibiting semantic commutativity. We show that, as with obstruction-freedom, every sequential object has a read-write conflict-free linearizable implementation. Our conflict-free universal construction is based on a novel generalization of the instrumental commit-adopt object, interesting in its own right.
item.dc:creator: Petr Kuznetsov, Pierre Sutra, Guillermo Toyos-Marfurt

item.title: Temporal Conductance and Bounds on the Voter Model for Dynamic Networks
item.description: arXiv:2606.13374v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The voter model is a classical stochastic process that models how opinions might spread through a network: at each step, every node lazily adopts the opinion of a random neighbour; eventually all nodes share the same opinion (consensus). Stronger connectivity should yield faster consensus. Berenbrink, Giakkoupis, Kermarrec, and Mallmann-Trenn (ICALP 2016) make this precise via the network's conductance: if the network has $m$ edges, minimum degree $d_{\min}$, and conductance at least $\phi$, then the voter model reaches consensus in expected $O(m/(d_{\min}\phi))$ steps. Their results extend to dynamic networks with fixed vertex degrees by considering the network's conductance at each time step. We introduce temporal conductance $\Phi$, a more general connectivity measure for dynamic networks. Unlike static conductance, which collapses to $0$ whenever some snapshot is disconnected, $\Phi$ captures connectivity through edges that appear at different times. We generalise the results of Berenbrink et al. from static conductance to temporal conductance, showing that the expected consensus time of the standard voter model is at most $O(m/(d_{\min}\Phi))$. Moreover, we prove that this bound is tight up to constant factors. We expect temporal conductance to be a useful primitive for analysing other dynamics on temporal networks, and potentially time-inhomogeneous Markov chains more generally.
item.dc:creator: Tatiana Rocha Avila, Holger Dell, John Lapinskas

item.title: AoiZora: Compiler-Agnostic, Placement-Aware Auto-Parallelization for Video Diffusion Transformers
item.description: arXiv:2606.17566v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Video diffusion transformers (DiTs) process tens of thousands of spatio-temporal tokens per denoising step, so low-latency inference and training commonly spread them across several accelerators. Auto-parallelization systems price a sharding on its logical graph, but its cost depends on the program the compiler generates and, on direct networks such as TPU sub-slices, on which chip runs each logical rank; both are visible only after compilation, while the chip assignment must be fixed before it. We present AoiZora, a compiler-agnostic auto-parallelization framework built on two IRs, one for the program a partitioner shards and one for the program a compiler emits; it chooses the logical mesh, the layout of every tensor and operation, and the device assignment of an unsharded model by pricing its compiled programs, without executing any candidate. At the core of AoiZora is evidence, a compiler-neutral record of a compiled program that leaves its placement open, so that one compilation can be priced under many placements by a calibrated model of the accelerator network and the placement can determine which sharding is selected. On TPU v5e, AoiZora reduces the denoising latency of Wan 2.1 and HunyuanVideo by 1.23x and 1.32x on average over expert configurations and Alpa, finding each plan within 10 minutes; it also speeds up training on TPU v5p by 1.11x on 4 chips and 1.21x on 8 chips on average and parallelizes PyTorch programs on GPUs with the same core.
item.dc:creator: Kaijian Wang, Yuanyuan Xu, Fanjiang Ye, Ye Cao, Jingwei Zuo, T. S. Eugene Ng, Yarong Mu, Yuke Wang

item.title: RouteBalance: Fused Model Routing and Load Balancing for Heterogeneous LLM Serving
item.description: arXiv:2606.17949v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Current heterogeneous LLM serving clusters decouple request scheduling into two independent tiers: learned model routers select a model based on the prompt without visibility into instance-level load, while load balancers assign requests to an instance of that chosen model without cross-model quality or cost awareness. This decoupled hierarchy induces conflicting objectives and severely restricts the global optimization space. For example, a quality-oriented router may stubbornly direct 55% of requests to a 72B model regardless of growing queues, inflating mean latency by 2.4$\times$ under high load. Conversely, a cost-minimizing router over-allocates traffic to the cheapest model, leaving capable instances underutilized and capping aggregate cluster throughput. This paper presents RouteBalance, a serving scheduler that unifies model routing and instance dispatching into a single decision. RouteBalance dynamically batches incoming requests into short, load-adaptive rounds. In each round, it amortizes quality and response-length estimation across candidate models, takes a single snapshot of all instance loads, and solves a normalized assignment problem balancing quality, cost, and estimated latency. On a 28-GPU heterogeneous cluster spanning four Qwen model sizes and diverse GPU architectures, RouteBalance Pareto-dominates 231 of 246 baseline configurations across quality, latency, and cost simultaneously. These baselines comprise combinations of two learned routers with four downstream dispatchers, as well as five standalone dispatchers. At iso-quality, per-rate median reductions across baselines are 23--60% in mean E2E latency and 26--37% in serving cost. Code: https://github.com/AKafakA/route-balance.
item.dc:creator: Wei Da, Evangelia Kalyvianaki

item.title: Splaxel: Efficient Distributed Training of 3D Gaussian Splatting for Large-scale Scene Reconstruction via Pixel-level Communication
item.description: arXiv:2606.18588v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables high-fidelity and real-time 3D scene reconstruction, but scaling training to large-scale scenes requires optimizing hundreds of millions of Gaussians across multiple GPUs. Existing distributed approaches either partition scenes into isolated regions, causing global inconsistency, or rely on global Gaussian-level exchanges, which lead to substantial growth in inter-GPU communication and quickly dominate iteration time. We propose Splaxel, a communication-efficient distributed 3DGS training framework based on pixel-level local rendering and global composition. Instead of synchronizing Gaussians, each GPU renders its local subset and exchanges only partial pixel values, maintaining mathematical consistency while keeping communication cost stable as the scene size increases. Splaxel further reduces pixel-level redundancy through geometric and transmittance visibility prediction and improves GPU utilization via conflict-free camera-view consolidation. Evaluated on large-scale datasets with up to 120M Gaussians, Splaxel achieves up to 7.6$\times$ speedup over the state-of-the-art distributed 3DGS framework while preserving high reconstruction quality.
item.dc:creator: Wenqi Jia, Zhewen Hu, Ying Huang, Jian Xu, Siyi Wu, Yangming Zhang, Yu Gong, Stavros Kalafatis, Yuke Wang, Wei Niu, Chengming Zhang, Ang Li, Sheng Di, Yuede Ji, Bo Fang, Miao Yin

item.title: OmniCast: Interaction-Aware Serving for Real-Time Omni-Modal LLMs
item.description: arXiv:2606.22983v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Realtime omni-modal LMs support speech-centric conversations where users stream inputs, hear generated audio, and interrupt freely. Existing Omni-LM serving systems still rely on throughput-oriented LLM scheduling and LRU KV offloading. These policies ignore audio playback and multi-turn reuse: they may generate tokens far beyond what users hear, wasting work after barge-in, and evict KV state needed in the next turn. OmniCast is an interaction-aware serving system for realtime Omni-LM interaction. It exposes playback progress, speech activity, and barge-in events to the serving pipeline. The scheduler prioritizes first-audio and near-underrun sessions while limiting generation beyond the playback frontier. The KV manager uses next-use-aware eviction and preloads likely-needed KV during user speech to hide reload latency. On vLLM-Omni, OmniCast improves realtime serving across two Omni-LMs and mixed workloads. It lowers P90 audio TTFP by $1.55\times$ on average and up to $2.21\times$, while improving completed-request throughput by $1.15\times$ on average and up to $1.56\times$, and moves most KV reload work off the next-turn critical path.
item.dc:creator: Xiangyu Zhi, Peiqi Yin, Sheng Guan, Chenguang Zheng, James Cheng, Xiao Yan

item.title: Scaling LLM Agent Tool Access: The MCP Gateway
item.description: arXiv:2607.15593v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on tool calling to complete tasks. Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes tool calling between LLM agents and tool providers. It reduces integration cost and drives rapid growth in tool scale. In production deployments, tool access becomes difficult to scale. On the tool provider side, legacy services are not directly callable through MCP; the rapid protocol development creates ongoing compatibility cost. On the agent side, the number of mounted tools is limited by the LLM context window and inference overhead; mounting a large tool set increases token usage and inference latency and can reduce task success rate. Moreover, for stateful MCP backends with multiple replicas, preserving session affinity increases client-side complexity. We present a cloud-scale MCP Gateway system. It breaks the direct-connect model on the data plane and offloads legacy service integration, consolidating incompatible MCP variants, access control, tool recommendation, and session-aware routing at the gateway. The conversion module supports 315 OpenAPI services in the cloud and integrates MCP transport variants. Session-aware routing decouples the scalability of the gateway layer and the MCP service layer. The hybrid retrieval engine sustains $\sim$98\% Top-15 recall; it scales agent tool access to 3{,}000+ tools with improved tool selection accuracy. We also share the lessons learned from deploying the gateway system in production.
item.dc:creator: Mingxin Li, Enge Song, Yueshang Zuo, Xiaodong Liu, Rong Wen, Qiang Fu, Gianni Antichi, Jian He, Jing Tie, Zhou Shao, Xiaobo Xue, Xiong Xiao, Luyao Zhong, Shaokai Zhang, Jiangu Zhao, Jianyuan Lu, Shize Zhang, Xiaoqing Sun, Changgang Zheng, Zihao Fan, Haonan Li, Tian Pan, Xiaomin Wu, Yang Song, Xing Li, Biao Lyu, Meng Li, Haipeng Dai, Guihai Chen, Shunmin Zhu

item.title: NeMo-DCR: Bit-Exact Delta-Compressed Refit for Scalable Agentic RL at Trillion-Parameter Scale
item.description: arXiv:2610.08430v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) disaggregates training from rollout into different clusters, so each policy update must reach rollout clusters before the next batch: a full 1T checkpoint takes 87.5 min between two AWS regions, yet only 1-2% of BF16 elements change their stored values per step. Concurrent systems use this sparsity but reimplement placement rules, assemble full tensors, rebuild values arithmetically, or rely on a cross-cluster collective, and none fully recovers from mid-refit failures. We present NeMo-DCR (Delta-Compressed Refit), which sends only changes yet gives receivers the bits of a dense refit. NeMo-DCR describes changes in the Hugging Face canonical coordinates that both sides already share and leaves their placement to the serving runtime's native loader. It projects over 96% of MoE weight bytes directly and converts the rest, under 4%. It encodes changes as compressible XOR masks for over 96% of these bytes and as overwrites where XOR masks cannot apply, streams them over object storage or a relay tree without a cross-cluster collective, and updates receivers in place, recovering from failures with overwrite retries and a joint commit. With real updates, NeMo-DCR is $7\times$ faster than AReaL-DTE. In 3% and 5% stress cases, 30B-1T refits are 12-40$\times$ faster than a transport-only full-checkpoint reference over the same object storage, and would make a synchronous Kimi K2 RL step 1.4-1.5$\times$ faster at 1T.
item.dc:creator: Songlin Jiang, Zhiyu Li, Terry Kong, Yu Yao, Youngeun Kwon, Bernard Nguyen, Ashwath Aithal, Mario Di Francesco

item.title: ATTUNE: Agentic Throughput Tuning for LLM Training
item.description: arXiv:2610.17528v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Training a large language model can occupy thousands of GPUs for weeks, and its speed depends on its recipe: how the model is split across GPUs, how memory is traded for compute, and which kernels and communication overlaps it uses. Finding a good recipe is still manual work for experts. Automated tuners search fixed lists of knobs and check only that a job runs, so they miss large gains and can ship changes that silently alter what the model learns. ATTUNE tunes any working recipe unattended within a GPU-hour budget. A coding agent, guided by lessons from past tuning runs, finds each run's bottleneck and changes one setting at a time, and a correctness gate outside the agent refuses changes known to alter training. ATTUNE is deployed in production at Amazon Ads, a business that reported $19.8 billion in revenue in Q2 2026. Its recipes train the models that power Amazon's Ads Agent. On three of the models it tunes, its recipes raise throughput per GPU by 1.7x on average and up to 3.9x over internal expert-tuned recipes. It also speeds up four of NVIDIA's benchmark recipes by 7-26% and held-out public recipes by up to 2.6x, and beats Bayesian optimization, random search and OptiCo, a recent LLM-agent tuner, at the same GPU-hour budget. We release ATTUNE at github.com/amazon-science/attune and OpenRecipes, a leaderboard of more than 60 verified recipes, at openrecipes.ai.
item.dc:creator: Leo Fan, Hongyang Wang, Wenbo Chen, Jingguo Liu, Xian Li, Xuan Wang, Ruochen Wen, Yiming Yan, Hao Wu, Yichuan Li, Qian Qu, Zheshen Wang, Benoit Dumoulin

item.title: UlaCache: Unified Logical Addressing for Sparse LLM Serving
item.description: arXiv:2610.29820v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Long-context inference in large language models (LLMs) imposes substantial memory requirements for the key-value (KV) cache. Token-selective sparse attention reduces attention computation and memory traffic, but KV entries must still be retained for future queries. KV storage capacity therefore remains a constraint on decoding concurrency. Combining GPU and CPU memory expands this capacity but requires efficient access across heterogeneous memory pools. We present UlaCache, a KV cache management system that provides unified logical addressing across GPU and CPU memory. Its logical-slot interface enables the inference engine to allocate, write, access, and release KV entries using stable identifiers across attention parallelism modes. UlaCache manages physical placement, residency, and transfers, updating address mappings after KV transfers. Parallel Bucketed LRU (PB-LRU) reduces the overhead of KV replacement by parallelizing recency updates and eviction-candidate selection within a GPU memory pool shared across requests. We evaluate UlaCache against state-of-the-art baselines. Under tensor-parallel attention (TP), UlaCache provides up to $11.4\times$ the usable KV cache capacity of HiSparse. For GLM-5.3 on eight H200 GPUs, UlaCache achieves peak decoding throughput of $1.10\times$ and $1.59\times$ that of HiSparse under data-parallel attention (DPA) and TP, respectively. For HY4 Preview on eight B300 GPUs, the corresponding throughput ratios are $1.27\times$ and $1.93\times$.
item.dc:creator: Isaac Zhu, Alan Cao, Hugh Yin, Rocky Wang, Orion Wang, Hscos Zhang, Jack Li, Jason Zhao

item.title: GearUp: DAG-aware Acceleration for Serverless Inference Serving via Slack-guided Pre-loading
item.description: arXiv:2610.38196v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Serverless platforms increasingly host machine learning (ML) inference workflows, modeled as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) of interdependent functions. Beyond container startup, each ML node must load libraries, model weights, and CUDA kernels before it can run. These costs accumulate along dependent DAG paths and place initialization on the end-to-end critical path. Existing systems optimize one half of this problem. DAG-agnostic pre-loading prepares nodes the request may never reach, wasting host and GPU memory. DAG-aware serving routes and scales whole functions, leaving the loading stages inside a node untouched. This paper presents GearUp, a serverless DAG inference serving system that removes ML-node loading from the end-to-end critical path at low resource cost. GearUp profiles the loading stages of each node and schedules them inside the slack time the DAG exposes, hiding initialization behind upstream execution. It reuses initialized instances within and across requests to avoid redundant cold starts. A probabilistic, traffic-adaptive keep-alive policy sets how long idle instances are retained, balancing memory cost against cold-start risk under bursty load. On the AMBER Alert and FINRA-ML workflows with NVIDIA L40S GPUs, GearUp reduces median end-to-end latency by 64.5% and 75.9% against SMIless, for median speedups of 3.1x and 10.0x over cold execution. Integrated GPU and host memory allocation fall by up to 83.9% and 94.6% against eager pre-loading in InstaInfer. GearUp achieves 4.2x strong scaling on four workers.
item.dc:creator: Qi Qi, Yifan Sui, Hanfei Yu, Hong Zhang, Hao Wang

item.title: DistOptimize: Automatic Optimization of Distributed Protocols
item.description: arXiv:2610.39017v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Distributed consensus and consistency protocols are difficult to reason about yet foundational to the cloud; as such, they often undergo a rigorous proof and formal verification process before deployment. The same level of rigor is rarely applied to protocol modifications, which occur frequently in production and threaten to compromise safety. In this paper, we introduce DistOptimize, an automatic optimizer for distributed protocols that uses well-known optimization techniques to modify existing protocols without the risk of safety violations. DistOptimize adapts throughput optimizations from academic languages to frameworks used in production, verifying the correctness of the rewrites in Rocq and automating their application through a combination of calibration and ILP-based search space navigation. Applied to both fundamental distributed protocols and protocols used at AWS, DistOptimize improves throughput by up to 4x while increasing latency by at most 0.3ms.
item.dc:creator: David Chu McElroy, Shadaj Laddad, Lucky Katahanas, Mingwei Samuel, Octavio Lomeli, Natacha Crooks, Joseph M. Hellerstein, Mohsen Lesani

item.title: Characterizing Performance Tradeoffs in Heterogeneous GPU-Wafer-Scale Accelerator Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.39222v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As AI accelerator architectures become increasingly diverse, integrating different architectures into a unified system is emerging as a new heterogeneous computing paradigm. GPUs and WSEs differ substantially in compute, memory, and communication organization, creating both architectural complementarity and additional overheads, yet how to translate this heterogeneity into practical performance gains remains unclear. To address this gap, we propose a hierarchical benchmarking methodology to characterize GPU--WSE heterogeneous execution and the conditions for exploiting complementarity, together with an analytical performance model that identifies when heterogeneity becomes a bottleneck and when it yields system-level performance gains.
item.dc:creator: Ziyu Hu, Zhijing Ye, Jiamin Wang, Zhiqing Zhong, Zhendong Mi, Shaoyi Huang, Weijian Zheng, Rajkumar Kettimuthu, Xiaodong Yu

item.title: Sandman: A Sandbox Service for Production Agentic Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.39711v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) needs stateful environments for tool execution and evaluation. Training jobs request thousands of environments in bursts that can overwhelm shared cluster services, while cancelled or timed-out requests can leave resources running. We present Sandman, a sandbox service built and operated at Amazon for large-scale agentic RL workloads in production on shared Kubernetes. A small daemon mounted into unmodified task images preserves files and processes across calls. Sandman paces creation requests, checks sandbox readiness, and retains cleanup responsibility after callers time out or cancel. Production deployments created 3.1 million sandboxes for 122 coding-agent training runs in two weeks. Peak production concurrency was 11,858 sandboxes. In one 10,000-request multi-client burst, Sandman made half the sandboxes usable in 116 seconds and all in 308 seconds. Full delivery took 44% less time than a tuned configuration of agent-sandbox, an open-source sandbox manager for Kubernetes. Sandman left no sandboxes at client exit. On software-engineering task images, median no-op command latency was 2.0 ms, compared with 14.3 ms for agent-sandbox and 203.5 ms for OpenSandbox. We also measure provisioning costs and sandbox delays within training runs, and report design trade-offs and operational lessons from production use and comparisons with three open-source systems. We will open-source Sandman's daemon, provider and pool.
item.dc:creator: Yiming Yan, Hongyang Wang, Wenbo Chen, Xuan Wang, Yichuan Li, Jingguo Liu, Xian Li, Leo Fan, Chen Qi, Siwei Li, Qianli Wu, Ruochen Wen, Qian Qu, Zheshen Wang, Benoit Dumoulin

item.title: Precomputed Dominant Resource Fairness
item.description: arXiv:2507.08846v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Dominant Resource Fairness (DRF) is a resource allocation scheme, addressing the problem of fair allocation of multiple resource types among users with heterogeneous demands for different types of resources. Based on Max-min Fairness, which is a well-established algorithm in the literature for allocating resources in single resource type scenarios, DRF generalises the main principle of maximising the minimum share given to any user to the multiple resource case. It has a number of desirable properties, such as Sharing Incentive, Envy-Freeness, Pareto Efficiency, and Strategy Proofness, that make it preferable over alternatives, and as such, it is widely adopted in distributed systems. In the present study, we revisit the original study and analyse the structure of the algorithm in closer view. The main contribution is an alternative algorithm, which approximates the DRF allocation in linear time, significantly improving over the original algorithm's pseudo-polynomial runtime. We name the new algorithm Precomputed Dominant Resource Fairness (PDRF), after its main working principle. We provide bounds for approximating the original algorithm, and critically evaluate the agreements of aforementioned properties, comparing DRF and PDRF over them. It turns out that there is an adversarial strategy which forces DRF to unfairly allocate more resources to users who submit inflated demands. PDRF, on the other hand, favouring smaller demands, penalises such adversarial behaviour and creates incentive for users to submit their minimal demands.
item.dc:creator: Serdar Metin

item.title: VoxServe: Streaming-Centric Serving System for Speech Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2602.00269v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Speech Language Models (SpeechLMs) are increasingly deployed for streaming speech generation, where audio playback must start quickly and never stall. Serving them requires running two very different model components on the same system. An autoregressive LLM backbone emits audio tokens, and a codec converts chunks of those tokens into waveforms. Existing systems run the two as separately scheduled stages, and therefore either serialize them, let them interfere, or strand capacity by placing them on separate devices. We observe that overlapping the backbone and the codec on separate parts of the GPU raises throughput. Although this increases codec latency, most chunks can tolerate it, as long as it neither lies on the critical path of time-to-first-audio (TTFA) nor causes a playback stall. Based on this insight, we present VoxServe, a SpeechLM serving system that allocates GPU resources according to the urgency of chunks. VoxServe executes work on three asynchronous lanes. The LM lane runs the backbone on a large partition of the GPU's streaming multiprocessors, the background codec lane runs on a small partition beside it, and the urgent lane uses the whole GPU. The scheduler queues each request to the LM lane and routes every chunk the backbone completes by its urgency. A request's first chunk and chunks close to their playback deadline go to the urgent lane, and the rest are batched on the background lane. On Qwen3-TTS, VoxServe sustains 1.5x the request rate of the best existing system at a 200ms TTFA target without playback stalls. The code of VoxServe is available at https://github.com/vox-serve/vox-serve.
item.dc:creator: Keisuke Kamahori, Rohan Kadekodi, Garv Ghai, Wei-Tzu Lee, Atindra Jha, Stephanie Wang, Arvind Krishnamurthy, Baris Kasikci

item.title: RaMP: Runtime-Aware Megakernel Polymorphism for Mixture-of-Experts
item.description: arXiv:2604.26039v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: LLM serving systems autotune their GPU kernels offline by timing candidate kernel configurations, like tile sizes, at a range of batch sizes. This works when the number of tokens determines a kernel's work, as in dense layers. However, we show that it does not hold for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers where the router decides how the tokens are split across experts and GPUs. We find that the best kernel configuration depends on this split, and not only on the number of tokens--under expert parallelism, choosing the configuration for each GPU's actual token distribution is up to 1.45x faster than the existing choice. The split is not known until the router runs, so it cannot be looked up in advance. Hence, we introduce RaMP, which chooses the kernel configuration at run time from the routing split itself. RaMP compiles top configurations into one polymorphic kernel, and a small cost model on the GPU picks among them in a few microseconds. On serving traffic its cost model was never fit on, the configurations RaMP's cost model chooses from the kernel's full configuration space are up to 1.45x faster than those vLLM's offline autotuner picks for the same kernel on batches of 128 tokens or more (1.27x over all batches), and within 3.5% of an exhaustive search that times every configuration. RaMP's kernel and choice together make the MoE layer up to 1.84x faster than vLLM's Triton MoE on batches of 128 tokens or more. In vLLM, under both tensor and expert parallelism, RaMP lowers time per output token by up to 1.11x over the fastest stock MoE backend.
item.dc:creator: Vyom Sharma, Debajyoti Datta

item.title: Streaming Right Multiplication over Grammar-Compressed Matrices: A Memory-Bounded GPU Engine for Genotype and Graph Data
item.description: arXiv:2607.24971v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Grammar-compressed matrices store a matrix's non-zero structure as a RePair straight-line program (SLP), supporting matrix-vector products in time and space proportional to the compressed size. We target the regime where this is decisive on a GPU: when the uncompressed matrix exceeds device memory, so footprint (not floating-point throughput) is the binding constraint. Our SLP is a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of out-degree 2, and the right product $y=Mx$ is a single bottom-up sweep (leaves to roots): a conflict-free gather. We make the grammar properly layered (every nonterminal child one level below its parent) via pass-through completion, which inserts identity nodes to carry values upward until consumed. This yields a streaming evaluation in which each level reads only the level below and writes the next, so the live set fits in two alternating read-only/write-only buffers instead of scaling with the whole grammar. On genotype matrices, where a polygenic score is exactly the right product $y=G\beta$, a CUDA implementation shows a clear space advantage: a device footprint 3.5 to 8 times smaller than a materialized cuSPARSE CSR baseline, single-vector times within a small factor of cuSPARSE, and consistently lower GPU energy. Because the sweep needs only an associative and commutative combine, the same engine evaluates any homomorphism into a commutative monoid over the grammar by swapping a small leaf/combine/emit policy; the same reachability sweep scales to a billion-edge Software Heritage graph (261 TB dense, 21 times smaller serialized than cuSPARSE's CSR). We frame this as an algorithm-engineering case study: structural metrics (depth, live-set width, completion cost) are measured, architecture-independent grammar properties, whereas time and energy are profiled on a single board.
item.dc:creator: Francesco Tosoni, Gabriele Mencagli

item.title: Collective Reasoning, Single-Writer Execution: Fusion-MoA for Long-Horizon Agents
item.description: arXiv:2609.26080v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Mixture-of-Agents systems combine several language models into a stronger response, but tool-using agents act over long horizons in which every step changes external state and the history keeps growing. We present Fusion-MoA, a serving architecture that brings multi-model collaboration into this loop through executor-anchored consultation. One Executor model holds the full context and emits every text and tool call; when consultation is admitted, three specialist models review its proposed next action through a compact view under a shared 120-second deadline. The fleet sits behind one OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so an unmodified agent client drives it as a single model. Fusion-MoA serves an in-car assistant and an in-car personal agent for intelligent cockpits and is deployed on MetaX C550 servers. Evaluated as four quantized open-weight models on five NVIDIA L40S GPUs and driven by Claude Code, it passes 78 of the 89 Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks, 16 more than its Executor alone and 29 more than a self-hosted quantized Kimi K3 on the same client. On the 63 tasks that both it and the API-served LongCat-2.5-Preview pass, it needs 14.5 minutes on average against 17.5. Specialist reviews use 0.4% of the Executor's tokens, and every tool call comes from the Executor.
item.dc:creator: Zongyou Yang, Yinghan Hou, Botao Su, Ercheng Zhao

item.title: Certified Splitting: Decidability and Anchor Supply for Maximal-Munch Tokenization
item.description: arXiv:2610.08854v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A certificate is a window of bytes with an origin inside it such that, wherever the window occurs in a completely tokenizable input, the token covering the window's final byte begins at that origin. Certification is decided from the token set alone, and a certificate's occurrences mark where work may soundly begin. This paper decides certification and applies it to cuts, edits and audits. It is decided two ways, online with a completeness cutoff for literal vocabularies and offline through an armed-run verifier for arbitrary regular token sets. Either route, under a declared window budget, yields the anchor inventory, with a counterexample on each refutation. Cutting a completely tokenizable input at certified anchors and scanning the chunks independently reproduces the sequential segmentation, with no speculation or fixup pass. A tokenizability-preserving byte substitution moves boundaries only strictly between the certified anchors witnessed in the unchanged bytes on either side of it. For tokens of length at most L, an edit at p moves no boundary at or below p - L + 1. Cutting at every occurrence of a delimiter is sound exactly when it occurs only at token starts, and cutting after every occurrence exactly when it occurs only at token ends. Two instruments follow. The anchor-free span of a finite certified inventory is decided bounded or not with its exact supremum, three for the UTF-8 shape; and a differential auditor decides whether two token sets place different boundaries on an input both tokenize, with a differing input. Every theorem carries an executable check. Every measurement is a named program's output or arithmetic on such outputs, and each program ships with the paper or is pinned by commit in the munch library. That library's threaded scanner splits the archived campaign corpus at certified anchors and reproduces the sequential boundary stream byte for byte.
item.dc:creator: Nicklas Nidh\"ogg

item.title: Temporal Liquidity Crossing for Blockchains: An EIP-1559 Extension for Admission Below the Base Fee
item.description: arXiv:2610.30595v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Transactions differ in how their value changes with execution time and relative position. Ethereum's EIP-1559 lets them compete through fee fields, but a fee bid gives no enforceable claim to an earlier position in the block, and no way to express willingness to accept a later one. Its base fee is a hard admission floor. We introduce temporal liquidity markets (TLM), a framework for crossing complementary temporal requirements: transactions seeking early-region execution (consumers) can fund transactions that opt into exclusion from that region (providers). Selected consumers complete within the early region and are ordered among themselves by authorization density, both validator-checked. In our block-local EIP-1559 extension, providers may be admitted below the base-fee floor. Under TLM regulation, funding-conditioned and capacity-capped provider gas is excluded from the ordinary EIP-1559 controller input. Counting it there instead raises the base fee and displaces ordinary demand at a positive base-fee fixed point. Exclusion lets the controller regulate ordinary demand at its original target and preserves the no-TLM ordinary allocation by construction; in synthetic experiments it raises total utilization with funded gas. Selected consumers pay their signed authorizations, which fund provider shortfalls; the surplus is burned. We state an adversary model with strategic senders and builders and prove eight properties under it, among them validator-checked rule validity, full burn of the base fee, and no subsidy. An inserted consumer bid cannot raise any other consumer's charge. With a provider fee-cap floor, a small, capped inclusion fee and a consumer allowance tied to funded provider gas by a large enough link ratio, no finite set of consumer bids or providers that the builder inserts raises its direct fee payoff.
